ECE 6390 / Spacecraft systems

Eclipse & battery

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how eclipse capacity and orbit-to-orbit energy balance constrain battery sizing.

A constant electrical load P over an eclipse of duration t uses Pt of bus energy. If discharge efficiency is ηd, the stored-energy reduction is Pt/ηd. Use watts and hours for watt-hours, or watts and seconds for joules.

During sunlight, only array power beyond the simultaneous load can recharge storage. The stored-energy gain is ηc(Pₐ − P)tₛ when the surplus is positive, with charging curtailed at full capacity.

Capacity determines whether one eclipse can be served. Sustainable operation also requires each orbit to replace its losses. A larger battery can delay a persistent energy deficit while the average deficit remains.

Example

A 100 W load for 30 minutes with ηd = 0.92 removes 54.3 Wh from storage. A recharge interval that returns only 40 Wh leaves a 14.3 Wh deficit per cycle.

    Practice

    1. The battery can serve the first eclipse, but its charge before each eclipse keeps falling. Which calculation should be checked next?

    Compare energy removed and replaced over a whole orbit.

    Check the sunlight surplus and charging/discharging efficiencies. Orbit-averaged recharge is insufficient; increasing usable capacity alone does not restore a sustainable energy balance.
